concepts.title: Beringia & Early Migration
concepts.contentHtml:
During the last ice age, sea levels were ~120 m lower; the Bering land bridge (Beringia) connected Siberia to Alaska. Humans crossed sometime in the late Pleistocene.

Long-standing 'Clovis-first' model placed arrival ~13,000 BP. Newer evidence pushes arrival earlier — possibly 16,000-25,000+ years ago. Footprints at White Sands (~22,000 BP) and tools at Bluefish Caves are at the older end.

Coastal migration along the Pacific (the 'kelp highway') may have been faster and earlier than inland routes.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.contentHtml:
Once in the Americas, humans spread rapidly south. Within a few thousand years, populations existed from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. Diverse environments — Arctic, plains, deserts, rainforest, mountain, coastal — produced enormously varied cultures.

Genetic evidence supports a primary migration with later additional waves (Inuit, Athabaskan-related groups). Some isolated populations developed distinctive linguistic and cultural traits over thousands of years.

concepts.title: Agriculture
concepts.contentHtml:
Indigenous Americans independently domesticated maize, beans, squash, potatoes, sweet potatoes, manioc/cassava, peppers, tomatoes, cocoa, peanuts, and dozens of other crops.

Maize (corn) was domesticated from teosinte in Mexico ~9000 BP. Through breeding it was transformed into a productive grain. Today maize feeds billions globally.

The 'three sisters' (maize, beans, squash) intercropping was a sophisticated agricultural system that maintained soil fertility and provided balanced nutrition. American crops transformed Old World agriculture after 1492.

title: The Maya
description: Mesoamerican civilization with mathematics, astronomy, and writing

concepts.title: Classic Maya
concepts.contentHtml:
Maya civilization spanned ~2000 BCE-1697 CE in modern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras. The Classic Period (~250-900 CE) saw urban city-states (Tikal, Palenque, Calakmul, Copán) connected by trade and warfare.

Maya developed sophisticated mathematics including the concept of zero, and three calendars (260-day, 365-day, and Long Count). Their astronomy predicted Venus cycles and solar eclipses to remarkable precision.

concepts.title: Maya Writing
concepts.contentHtml:
The Maya developed the Americas' most sophisticated writing system — a complex logosyllabic script. Inscriptions on stelae, codices, and pottery record dynasties, alliances, wars, rituals.

Spanish missionaries destroyed nearly all Maya codices in the 16th century, considering them 'works of the devil'. Only four survive today.

Decipherment progressed slowly through the 20th century, accelerating dramatically after Russian linguist Yuri Knorozov's insights in the 1950s. Today most Maya texts can be read.

concepts.title: Classic Maya Collapse
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 800-900 CE, many southern Maya cities were abandoned. Population declined catastrophically; political systems collapsed.

Causes debated and probably multifactorial: drought (high-resolution paleoclimate records show several severe multi-decade droughts), warfare, environmental degradation, political failure.

Northern Yucatán Maya states (Chichén Itzá, Mayapán) flourished after the southern collapse. Maya descendants — millions of them speaking ~30 Maya languages — still live across Mesoamerica today.

concepts.title: Rise of Tenochtitlan
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco. Within ~150 years, they led the Aztec Triple Alliance (with Texcoco and Tlacopan) that dominated central Mexico.

At its 1500 peak, Tenochtitlan held 200,000+ people — among the world's largest cities. Causeways, aqueducts, and chinampas (floating gardens) supported it. Spanish conquistadors compared it favorably to European capitals.

concepts.title: Aztec Society
concepts.contentHtml:
Stratified society: nobles, priests, warriors, merchants (pochteca), artisans, commoners, slaves. Rich religious life with a pantheon centered on Huitzilopochtli (war/sun) and others.

Tribute from conquered city-states sustained the empire. Discontent among tributaries would prove crucial — many joined Cortés against the Aztecs.

Human sacrifice was a real and substantial part of Aztec religion. Spanish accounts exaggerated for propaganda, but the practice itself is well-documented archaeologically.

concepts.title: Spanish Conquest
concepts.contentHtml:
Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519. Allied with Tlaxcala and other anti-Aztec polities, plus enslaved interpreter La Malinche, he marched on Tenochtitlan.

Smallpox arrived in 1520 — devastating Indigenous populations who had no immunity. Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 after a long siege.

The conquest was not a few hundred Spaniards defeating millions — it was a massive Indigenous coalition led by Spanish capitalizing on Aztec rivalries, and crucially aided by epidemic disease.

title: The Inca Empire
description: Andean state with no writing but vast organization

concepts.title: Tawantinsuyu
concepts.contentHtml:
The Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu — 'Land of Four Quarters') stretched from modern Ecuador to Chile by 1500 — the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas. Capital: Cusco.

Built in just ~100 years, it integrated dozens of conquered peoples through a sophisticated road network (~40,000 km of roads), tribute system, and resettlement policies.

concepts.title: Engineering & Administration
concepts.contentHtml:
Inca road system included rope bridges, paved sections, and tampu (way stations) for messengers and travelers. Chasquis (relay runners) carried messages across the empire in days.

Without a writing system, the Inca used quipus — knotted strings — for record-keeping. Modern research shows quipus encoded numerical and possibly narrative information.

Stone masonry at sites like Sacsayhuamán fits massive blocks together without mortar with seams a knife can't penetrate. Inca engineering remains a subject of research and admiration.

concepts.title: Pizarro & Collapse
concepts.contentHtml:
The Inca emperor Atahualpa had just won a civil war when Francisco Pizarro arrived in 1532. Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca, demanded a roomful of gold and silver as ransom, then executed him anyway.

Spanish forces took advantage of Inca civil war exhaustion and rampant smallpox. Cusco fell in 1533. Indigenous resistance continued in remote refuges for decades.

Inca culture persists in modern Andean countries. Quechua is spoken by ~10 million people. Cusco and Machu Picchu draw millions of visitors annually.

title: North American Civilizations & Columbian Exchange
description: Mississippian cultures and ecological consequences of contact

concepts.title: Mississippian Cultures
concepts.contentHtml:
Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was a major North American urban center from ~1050-1350 CE — at its peak, the largest city north of Mexico, with perhaps 20,000-40,000 inhabitants.

Mississippian cultures built earthen mounds (Monks Mound at Cahokia is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork in North America), had stratified societies, and traded extensively.

Cahokia declined before European contact. Other Mississippian-derived cultures (Natchez, Caddo) persisted into European-contact era and influenced Indigenous nations the colonizers met.

concepts.title: Indigenous North America
concepts.contentHtml:
Pre-contact North America hosted hundreds of distinct nations and language families. The Pacific Northwest had complex hierarchical societies (Haida, Kwakwaka'wakw); the Southwest had Pueblo cultures; the Northeast had Iroquois and Algonquian peoples; the Plains had pre-horse hunting cultures.

The Iroquois Confederacy (Haudenosaunee) — five nations united under the Great Law of Peace — has been argued (controversially) as one influence on US constitutional thought.

Population estimates for the pre-contact Americas range widely (15-100+ million); North America alone may have had 5-10+ million people.

concepts.title: The Columbian Exchange
concepts.contentHtml:
Contact between Old and New Worlds after 1492 caused the largest ecological exchange in history. Crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chocolate, tobacco, peppers, peanuts) flowed east; horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, wheat, sugar flowed west.

Diseases — smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus — caused catastrophic mortality among Indigenous populations who had no immunity. Estimates of Indigenous population decline range 50-90%+ over the first century of contact.

The Columbian Exchange transformed Eurasia (potato-fueled population boom in Europe, chili peppers reshaping Asian cuisine) and the Americas (cattle ranching, equestrian Plains culture, demographic catastrophe). It remade the world.
